title: The run dispatches one tick at a time: max_parallel is read, reported, and never obeyed
description:
[orchestration] max_parallel = 4 is declared in .tick/runners.toml, validated by runconfig, and loaded into r.hostWidth at internal/reconcile/reconcile.go:782 - and its only consumer is internal/reconcile/profiles.go:256, which uses it to PRINT wave-width lines into the feed. The run loop itself is 'for _, entry := range plan { r.processTick(ctx, entry) }' at internal/reconcile/reconcile.go:1140: one tick start to finish - dispatch, wait, collect, merge, full gate, close - before the next is dispatched. There is no goroutine anywhere in reconcile.go or dispatch.go.

Measured on run epic-9pd's own feed, 18 closed ticks, dispatched->closed: median 53 min, mean 163. The gate is roughly 6 of those minutes; the rest is a worker thinking in its own worktree, which is the embarrassingly parallel part.

The integration half must stay serialized - there is one integration branch, and a gate that ran on a different tree proves nothing. So the shape is: dispatch and wait concurrently up to the declared width, and keep collect/integrate/gate/close/cleanup strictly one at a time, in settlement order.

The hazard this must not create is the one this epic has already produced three times (FETCH_HEAD, refs/remotes/<remote>/<branch>, the shared per-run peek ref): process-global git state touched by two writers at once. Concurrency inside ONE process reaches the same refs through one runstate.Store whose fetchID is per-instance, not per-goroutine.
notes:
2026-09-17 14:10 - Design decision, changed during implementation: on a refusal the run STOPS rather than draining the window.

Draining was the first instinct - the in-flight attempts are paid for, why abandon them? - but it is wrong. A failing gate leaves its tick's merge on the integration branch (that is what makes the documented repair 'fix the tree and run again'), so any attempt drained after it would gate against a tree already known to be bad and fail for a reason that has nothing to do with its own work. A run that manufactures failures for good work is worse than one that stops.

And nothing is lost by stopping: an in-flight attempt is durable - marker on the remote, commits on its own branch - and a resumed run adopts it by identity. That is not a hope; it is what happened to attempt 22 of 7zs this morning, dispatched by one incarnation and adopted, collected and closed by the next.

The acceptance item that said in-flight attempts are 'drained through their own gates rather than abandoned' is therefore replaced by: a refusal stops further dispatch, and every attempt still in flight is NAMED in the feed as still running and adoptable on resume.
2026-09-17 20:31 - Operator-visible consequence of the window, found by the gate: attempt numbers get sparser per tick.

Attempt numbers are run-wide - they count the run's dispatches - so which number a tick's second try receives depends on how many OTHER dispatches the run made first. At width 1 a tick's k-th try was reliably attempt k. At width N it is not: in the fixture a2 takes number 2, so a1's second try is attempt 3.

Nothing about identity or the ladder changes - the branch, marker and settle argument are still named by the unique run-wide number, and the derivation still says 'escalated 1 rung(s) after 1 failed attempt(s)'. But anything that assumed try k == attempt k was relying on width one. TestAFailedAttemptEarnsTheNextRung did, and now asks for a try ordinal instead.

Worth checking before the next widened run: any operator doc or message that reads a try count off an attempt number.
acceptance_criteria: A run with max_parallel = N > 1 has up to N attempts dispatched and waiting at the same time, proven by a test that observes overlapping dispatch/settlement windows in the feed. Collect, integrate, gate, close and cleanup are serialized: a test proves no two ticks integrate or gate concurrently. go test -race passes on internal/reconcile. max_parallel = 1 and an absent max_parallel both behave exactly as the sequential run does today. A refusal stops further dispatch, and attempts already in flight are drained through their own gates rather than abandoned.
